objective: Know the risk factors a suicide lethality assessment looks for -- a detailed plan, access to means, past attempts -- and report any suicidal statement to the RN at once
secondaryObjectives: Collect data on the client's potential for violence to self or others, and report warning signs immediately

sources.cite: NIMH, Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (ASQ) Toolkit, information sheet: four questions and a fifth acuity question asked after any yes; a yes to it is an acute positive, 'imminent risk', that needs a STAT safety and full mental health evaluation, and the patient 'cannot leave until evaluated for safety'; a non-acute positive needs a brief suicide safety assessment; refusing to answer counts as positive
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in NIMH's PDF (summarizing fetch with short quotes). The four questions: a wish to be dead, feeling others would be better off, thoughts of suicide in the past week, any attempt ever. 'Clinical judgment can always override a negative screen.' Validated for youth and adult medical patients, including adult medical inpatients (Horowitz et al., Psychosomatics 2020); the toolkit has emergency department, inpatient and outpatient pathways (NIMH adult toolkit page, read the same day). The questions are paraphrased in the sim.

sources.cite: NIMH, Adult ASQ Toolkit: Brief Suicide Safety Assessment guides, nursing scripts and suicide risk screening pathways for the emergency department, the inpatient medical/surgical unit and outpatient primary care and specialty clinics
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch): an index page; the pathways themselves were not opened, so what each setting does after a positive screen is taken from the information sheet.

sources.cite: The Joint Commission, R3 Report Issue 18: National Patient Safety Goal for suicide prevention, NPSG.15.01.01 (effective 2019-07-01): EP1 environmental risk assessment; EP2 screen 'using a validated screening tool'; EP3 an assessment that 'directly asks about suicidal ideation, plan, intent, suicidal or self-harm behaviors'; EP4 document the risk level and the mitigation plan; EP5-EP7 policies for monitoring, discharge counseling and follow-up
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; issue dated 2019-11-20, updated 2025-12-03). The report names one-to-one monitoring as a key protocol on nonpsychiatric units; it does not itself require it, so the observation level in each sim is the facility's policy.

sources.cite: The Columbia Lighthouse Project, Columbia Protocol (C-SSRS) triage page: 'the most worrisome answers are a recent (past month) yes to items 4 or 5' (intent, intent with a plan) 'and/or any recent (3 months) behavior'; next steps 'are setting specific', and 'interventions should be changed to reflect your individual resources and policies'
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; page last modified 2024-03-22). The screener's items, relayed from the NCMHCE session (read 2026-11-11): wish to be dead; suicidal thoughts; thoughts with method; intent without plan; intent with plan; suicidal behavior.

brief.situation: Harold Fenn, 79 (a fictional client), is in a skilled nursing facility for rehabilitation after a hip fracture. His wife moved into memory care last month. At 08:40, as you bring his morning medications, he pushes the tray away and says, 'What's the point. I'm no use to anyone now. I want to die.' You are his licensed practical nurse; the RN supervisor is on the other wing, and a nursing assistant is down the hall. You have about 30 minutes before your medication pass must go on.
handover: Hip fracture repair three weeks ago; walking with a walker in therapy; eating poorly this week.
Facility policy: any suicidal statement is reported to the RN at once, in person or by phone, without leaving the client alone; the client stays in sight of staff until the RN assesses.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and do from the action groups. Harold answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His trust, distress and how much he discloses change with what you say. Your role is to collect data, keep him safe and report to the RN.
Your time ends at 30 minutes. Afterward you write a short summary, then document what you found and what you did.

source.note: About 30 minutes before the morning medication pass must continue (author's scenario timing).
How trust and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a patient.

formulation.question: Write your summary for the RN: what Harold said, the data you collected, and what you did.

parts.label: Data
parts.criteria: Gives his exact words and the data: a wish to be dead, feeling a burden, suicidal thoughts this week, has thought about a plan, possible access at the bedside, no past attempts; recent losses (his wife's memory care move, his fracture); his son.
parts.modelAnswer: He said, 'I'm no use to anyone now. I want to die.' He wishes he were dead, feels a burden and has had suicidal thoughts this week; he has thought about a plan and may have access at the bedside; no past attempts. His wife moved to memory care last month and he is recovering from a hip fracture. His son visits Sundays.

parts.label: Actions
parts.criteria: Names staying with him, reporting to the RN at once by phone, the drawer checked with him, the handoff, and no promise of secrecy.
parts.modelAnswer: I stayed with him and phoned the RN at once; with him, I checked the bedside drawer and removed what did not belong; the nursing assistant sat with him when I had to step away; I gave the RN a bedside handoff with his exact words.

source.note: Trust at the close of the conversation.

scoring.modelReasoning: Within the practical nurse's role, a suicidal statement means: ask directly, collect the data the RN's assessment needs (a plan, access, past attempts), keep the client in sight and report to the RN at once without leaving him. Secrecy is never promised, and the RN takes over the assessment.
